messages.subject: Re: [TMB users] Thin-plate splines (GAM) in TMB: high memory usage
messages.subject_clean: [TMB users] Thin-plate splines (GAM) in TMB: high memory usage
messages.body_plain:
"I'd be curious if there's another way around this using batches."

The batch approach can in theory be implemented using atomic functions. You need to create an atomic function that evaluates the likelihood for one batch (batch size 1 might be best). The idea is outlined in this example:
https://github.com/kaskr/adcomp/blob/master/tmb_examples/register_atomic.cpp
However, I don't know how well it performs for your model.

On Monday, July 26, 2021 at 6:48:05 PM UTC+2 samuel.vj...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hi all,
>
> Kasper's prediction appears to have panned out with respect to the simulated data. Here are the estimated (+/- 1.95 * SD) for the "batches" and "no batches" models. The gradients at convergence are also completely different as well.
>
>
> However, both approaches "somewhat" approximated the true values. I'd be curious if there's another way around this using batches. I haven't tried using tmbad.sparse_hessian_compress from experimental branch yet.
>
> Thanks,
> SR
>
> On Friday, July 16, 2021 at 3:38:59 AM UTC-6 kasper.k...@gmail.com wrote:
> > Nice idea, but I'm sorry to say that it doesn't work (unless I'm overlooking something... I hope I am!).
> >
> > You cannot apply Laplace for each batch and then sum up because
> > log( integrate exp(f1(u)+f2(u)) du )
> > is not in general equal to
> > log( integrate exp(f1(u)) du ) + log( integrate exp(f2(u)) du )
> >
> > Hardly relevant if the approach doesn't work, but pay special attention to this line of the DATA_UPDATE documentation:
> > "Updatable data items behave like parameters. In particular, if-else branching on such data should be avoided."
> > which means that the branch:
> > if(usePenalty==1){ ... }
> > won't behave as expected when 'usePenalty' is updated.
> >
> >
> > On Friday, July 16, 2021 at 12:17:15 AM UTC+2 samuel.vj...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > Success!
> > >
> > > Hans' approach to splitting up the data into batches on the R side worked. I made a new objective and gradient function that swaps out the data for each batch and then accumulates the objective function/gradient. I've attached an update example that shows how I did it. The functions could probably be modified or improved (parallelized?), but the basic version works!

> > > Something like this -- maybe just a simple linear model -- would also be nice to have on the tmb-case-studies repository, in case other people are working with large datasets and need some way to break it into bits.

messages.subject: Large gradients at parameter vector estimate
messages.subject_clean: Large gradients at parameter vector estimate
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am trying to fit a nonlinear mixed effects model with 14 parameters to a collection of 100 simulated time series. The model being estimated and the generative model are identical, so I know the true parameter vector `p`. For this simulated data set, BFGS converges to a reasonable approximation `p_hat` of `p`, but `obj$gr(p_hat)` is extremely large: the elements had minimum order 1e+8 and maximum order 1e+10.

I wondered whether the problem was with `obj$gr`, so I tried evaluating `gr2(p_hat1)`, where `gr2` is just computing a central difference approximation of the gradient using `obj$fn`. The result had maximum order 1e+6.

I also tried refitting the model using `gr2` instead of `obj$gr`, and this produced a `p_hat2` comparable to `p_hat`. `obj$gr(p_hat2)` had maximum order 1e+3, and `gr2(p_hat2)` had maximum order 1e+2.

I guess I have a few general questions:
- What is causing the large gradients, and the discrepancies between `obj$gr` and `gr2`?
- How can I approach diagnosing/stabilizing the problem, to obtain a fit with a useful Hessian?

I've attached an MRE. Any input is greatly appreciated.

Thanks,
Mikael

messages.body_plain:
I took some advice from a different thread and tried fixing some parameters with `map` until the problem went away. Fixing two specific correlation parameters to their true values gets me reasonable (maximum order 1e-1) gradients, which suggests that it's probably a good idea to regularize all of the correlation parameters in the template.

I _am_ still puzzled by the original issue. Is there an answer to why the gradients were so large, even though the function evaluations were OK/of stable magnitude?

Mikael

messages.subject: Efficient computation in TMB of sum(diag(X %*% solve(Y))) for n-by-n SPD X,Y
messages.subject_clean: Efficient computation in TMB of sum(diag(X %*% solve(Y))) for n-by-n SPD X,Y
messages.body_plain:
If I had the matrices X and invY already, then in the template I would just do something like

Type traceXinvY = (X.array() * invY.transpose().array()).sum();

However, if I am starting from the UNSTRUCTURED_CORR parametrization of SPD matrices, where instead of matrix X I have a vector x = c(log_sd, theta) (and likewise for Y), then what would be the most efficient way to compute the desired trace?

Certainly, I could construct X and Y and use atomic::matinvpd, but I feel like there might be a better way?

Thanks,
Mikael
